French and Kinyarwanda reach the same shape for different reasons. This is the concept that owns 'blue'; EX04 was corrected to 'changed colour' so the two stay distinguishable.

suggested_french: J'ai une douleur ecrasante dans la poitrine et elle descend dans le bras.
suggestion_note: KEPT 'ecrasante', AND THE MEASUREMENT IS NARROWER THAN THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS NOTE CLAIMED. CR01/EX05 are the only pair in the corpus with a recorded distinguishing axis — jaw-or-arm against arm alone — so they must not land in one phrase group. Run through the real splitter rule, the union is one wording away rather than already present: v1-faithful EX05 ('...qui va vers le bras') joins a CR01 phrased in parallel ('...qui va vers la machoire ou vers le bras'), and does NOT join sheet draft D050's 'qui monte vers'. Two independent things keep the drafted pair apart — this row says 'et elle descend' rather than 'qui va', and CR01 opens on 'lourde' rather than on 'une douleur ecrasante'. Either alone suffices; both are kept because of what this pair is. The 'lourde' choice stands on its own ground anyway: it is the speaker's own lexical separation, 'igituza kimuremereye' against 'harandya cyane'.

suggested_french: Quand {REL} respire a fond, sa poitrine lui fait mal.
suggestion_note: 'lui' is INVARIABLE in French — the indirect-object pronoun carries no gender — so the construction English had to solve with singular 'their' costs French nothing. Second place in this domain where French is freer than English, and the first where it is freer than Kinyarwanda, whose third here needs 'hamubabaza'.
